question:
With the strong failure detector S, for how many crash failures can consensus be solved, and what property of the detector makes this possible?
A) Up to $n-1$ failures, because no non-faulty process is ever suspected by anybody.
B) Up to $n-1$ failures, because some non-faulty process is eventually never suspected by anybody after an unknown initial period.
C) Up to $n-1$ failures, because some non-faulty process is never suspected by anybody.
D) Only fewer than $n/2$ failures, because some non-faulty process is never suspected by anybody.
atom_statement: With the strong failure detector S, consensus can be solved for any number of failures, up to $n-1$. This works because some non-faulty process $c$ is never suspected by anybody.
evidence: With the strong failure detector S, we can solve consensus for any number of failures.
However, there is some non-faulty process c that nobody every suspects, and this is enough to solve consensus with as many as n −1 failures.

key_points: P can solve terminating reliable broadcast
S cannot
◇P cannot
question: Which of the failure detector classes P, S, and ◇P are sufficient to solve terminating reliable broadcast in an asynchronous system with crash failures, and which are not?
atom_statement: Terminating reliable broadcast cannot be solved with S or with ◇P, although it can be solved with P.
evidence: It’s not hard to see that we can’t solve terminating reliable broadcast with either S or ♦P.

question:
True or False?
"If a majority of processes may crash ($f \ge n/2$), consensus cannot be solved using only ◇P, and hence not with ◇S either. The reason is that ◇P may give wrong output for an arbitrarily long initial interval, yet consensus must still terminate, so a partition-style argument applies."
atom_statement: Consensus cannot be solved with only ◇P, and therefore not with ◇S, when a majority of processes may fail ($f \ge n/2$). ◇P can mislead the processes for a long initial interval, and consensus must still terminate, so a partition argument applies.
evidence: We can show that with a majority of failures, we’re in trouble with just ♦P (and thus with ♦S, which is trivially simulated by ♦P).
The reason is that ♦P can lie to us for some long initial interval of the protocol, and consensus is required to terminate eventually despite these lies.

question:
A system provides only a failure detector of class ◇P. A protocol designer wants to run an algorithm that requires a detector of class S (some non-faulty process is never suspected by anybody, starting from the beginning). The designer asks whether some transformation algorithm running on top of the ◇P detector can always simulate a detector of class S.
Can ◇P be used in this way to simulate S? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: The lattice of classes does not collapse: ◇P cannot simulate S, S cannot simulate ◇P, and ◇S cannot simulate any of the other classes.
evidence: What is trickier is to show that this structure doesn’t collapse: ♦P can’t simulate S, S can’t simulate ♦P, and ♦S can’t simulate any of the other classes.

key_points: Behaves like a collection of $n$ single-writer multi-reader atomic registers
Snapshot operation returns what appears to be the state of all $n$ registers at the same time
question: In shared-memory distributed computing, what is an atomic snapshot object, and what does its special snapshot operation return?
atom_statement: An atomic snapshot object acts like a collection of $n$ single-writer multi-reader atomic registers, with a special snapshot operation that returns what appears to be the state of all $n$ registers at the same time.
evidence: An atomic snapshot object acts like a collection of n single-writer multi-reader atomic registers with a special snapshot operation that returns (what appears to be) the state of all n registers at the same time.

question:
True or False?
"A wait-free atomic snapshot protocol only needs to let a process finish its own snapshot or write provided that all the other processes keep running."
atom_statement: A wait-free atomic snapshot protocol must let any process finish its own snapshot or write even if all the other processes lock up.
evidence: But it gets harder if we want a protocol that is wait-free, where any process can ﬁnish its own snapshot or write even if all the others lock up.

question:
A system has 5 processes sharing an atomic snapshot object. In the implementation, processes 2 through 5 may crash at arbitrary points, including in the middle of their own operations. Process 1 is guaranteed to complete any snapshot or write it starts after a finite number of its own steps, no matter which of the other four processes have crashed or stopped taking steps.
Does this implementation meet the wait-free progress requirement for process 1's snapshot and write operations? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: A wait-free atomic snapshot protocol must let any process finish its own snapshot or write even if all the other processes lock up, which makes it harder than the failure-free case where the whole register file can simply be locked, read, and unlocked.
evidence: This is easy without failures: we simply lock the whole register ﬁle, read them all, and unlock them to let all the starving writers in.
But it gets harder if we want a protocol that is wait-free, where any process can ﬁnish its own snapshot or write even if all the others lock up.

key_points: At most $n+1$ collects
To avoid two identical collects, the adversary must supply a new value in every collect after the first
Only $n-1$ other processes can each supply one new value before some process shows a second new value, which ends the snapshot
question: In the helping-based atomic snapshot algorithm with $n$ processes, how many collects can a single snapshot operation take before it is guaranteed to terminate, and why?
atom_statement: A snapshot operation in the helping algorithm terminates after at most n+1 collects, because to avoid the identical-collects case the adversary must supply a new value in every collect after the first, but can supply only one new value for each of the n−1 other processes before some process shows a second new value.
evidence: trying to do snapshots all the time, a snapshot operation of a single process is guaranteed to terminate after at most n + 1 collects.
The reason is that in order to prevent case (a) from holding, the adversary has to supply at least one new value in each collect after the ﬁrst.
But it can only supply one new value for each of the n −1 processes that aren’t doing collects before case (b) is triggered (it’s triggered by the ﬁrst process that shows up with a second new value).
Adding up all the collects gives 1 + (n −1) + 1 = n + 1 collects before one of the cases holds.

Values written to the registers are tagged with increasing sequence numbers. A process repeats collects (reads of all $n$ registers) until two successive collects return exactly the same vector of values and sequence numbers. What can be concluded?
A) At least one of those values was present in its register at some time between the two collects.
B) Each of those values was present in its register at some time between the two collects, but they were not necessarily present at the same time.
C) Exactly those values were all present in the registers simultaneously, but only at some time before the first collect began.
D) Exactly those values were all present in the registers simultaneously at some time between the two collects.
atom_statement: If values are tagged with increasing sequence numbers and a process repeats collects (reads of all n registers) until two successive collects return exactly the same vector of values and sequence numbers, then precisely those values were present in the registers at some time between the two collects.
evidence: Let’s tag any value written with a sequence number, so that each value written has a seqno ﬁeld attached to it that increases over time.
Suppose now that we repeatedly perform collects—reads of all n registers—until two successive collects return exactly the same vector of values and sequence numbers.
values were present in the registers at some time in between the two collects.

question:
In a 4-process system using the Afek et al. snapshot algorithm, process 1 is scanning. Its first collect shows process 2 with sequence number 5 and process 3 with sequence number 8. Its second collect shows process 2 with sequence number 6 and process 3 with sequence number 8. Its third collect shows process 2 with sequence number 6 and process 3 with sequence number 9. Process 4's sequence number is unchanged throughout.
Can the scan terminate after the third collect, either as a direct scan or as an indirect scan? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: In the Afek et al. algorithm a scan repeats collects until either two successive collects are identical (a direct scan, returning that collect) or it has seen three different sequence numbers from the same process (an indirect scan, returning the snapshot embedded in the second of those writes).
evidence: So a snapshot repeatedly does collects until either (a) it gets two identical collects, in which case it can return the results (a direct scan, or (b) it sees three diﬀerent values from the same process, in which case it can take the snapshot collected by the second write (an indirect scan).

key_points: Cannot conclude the other process did not write its bit, since it may have made a stale write that did not change the value

question: In the handshake mechanism used for snapshots, a checker reads another process's handshake bit and finds the same value as in its previous read (checkHandshake returns false). What can and cannot be concluded about the other process's activity?
atom_statement: In the handshake mechanism, a checkHandshake that returns false does not guarantee that the other process did not write its bit, since it may have made a stale write that did not change the value. It guarantees only that the other process did not perform both a read and a write since the checker's previous read.

question:
True or False?
"The simple snapshot scheme of repeating collects until two successive collects are identical may fail to terminate when many writers are active, so writers must be slowed down or made to help by performing snapshots themselves."
atom_statement: The simple scheme of repeating collects until two are identical does not terminate when there are many writers, so writers must be slowed down or made to help by doing snapshots themselves.
evidence: Unfortunately, it doesn’t terminate if there are a lot of writers around.1 So we need some way to slow the writers down, or at least get them to do snapshots for us.

A shared array has 8 single-writer registers, and 7 writer processes continuously update their own registers in an unending loop. Is the scanner's snapshot guaranteed to terminate? (Yes/No)

evidence: Unfortunately, it doesn’t terminate if there are a lot of writers around.1 So we need some way to slow the writers down, or at least get them to do snapshots for us.

key_points: For any complete concurrent execution there exists a sequential execution with the same operations and return values
The total order of operations in that sequential execution is a linearization of (is consistent with and extends) the partial order of operations in the concurrent execution
question: What does it mean for an implementation of a shared object to be linearizable? Describe the condition in terms of its concurrent executions and a corresponding sequential execution.
atom_statement: An implementation of an object is linearizable if, for any complete concurrent execution of the object, there is a sequential execution with the same operations and return values whose total order of operations is a linearization of the partial order of operations in the concurrent execution.
evidence: The strongest consistency property generally used is lineariz- ability [HW90], which says roughly that an implementation of an object is linearizable if, for any complete concurrent execution of the object, there is a sequential execution of the object with the same operations and return values, where the (total) order of operations in the sequential execution is a linearization of the (partial) order of operations in the concurrent execution.

question:
True or False?
"In a concurrent execution $H$, the partial order $<_H$ on operations is defined by $a <_H b$ when the invoke event of operation $a$ precedes the invoke event of operation $b$ in $H$."
atom_statement: The partial order $<_H$ on operations in a concurrent execution $H$ is defined by $a <_H b$ when the response event of operation $a$ precedes the invoke event of operation $b$ in $H$.
evidence: The order in each case is deﬁned as a <H b if the response event for opera- tion a in execution H precedes the invoke event for operation b in the same execution.

question:
A shared atomic register initially holds 0. In a complete concurrent execution $H''$, process $p$ invokes write(1) at time 1 and receives its response at time 4. Process $q$ invokes read at time 2 and receives the response 0 at time 3. Process $r$ then invokes read at time 5 and receives the response 1 at time 6. Consider the sequential execution $S$ consisting of, in this order: $q$'s read returning 0, $p$'s write(1), $r$'s read returning 1.
Is $S$ a linearization of $H''$? (Yes/No)

Obtain the sequential execution by treating every operation as occurring atomically at its linearization point, consistent with the object's specification
question: Besides directly constructing a sequential execution whose order extends the real-time partial order, what alternative method can be used to show that an execution is linearizable, and how is the sequential execution obtained under it?
atom_statement: Linearizability can alternatively be shown by assigning each operation a linearization point between its invocation and response. The sequential execution $S$ is then obtained by treating every operation as occurring atomically at its linearization point, consistent with the object's specification.
evidence: An alternative method is to assign each operation a linearization point somewhere between when its invocation and response, and obtain S by assuming that all operations occur atomically at their linearization points is consistent with the speciﬁcation of the object; this is equivalent to constructing <S⊇<H since given <S we can always ﬁnd consistent linearization points.

options.B: If $H|A$ is sequentially consistent for each object $A$, then $H$ is linearizable.
options.C: If $H|A$ is linearizable for each object $A$, then $H$ is guaranteed only to be sequentially consistent, not necessarily linearizable.
options.D: If $H|A$ is linearizable for each object $A$, then $H$ is linearizable.

question:
Let $H$ be an execution involving several objects, and let $H|A$ denote its restriction to operations on object $A$. Which statement correctly expresses the composability of linearizability?
A) If $H|A$ is linearizable for each object $A$, then $H$ is linearizable only when all objects are accessed by the same single process.
B) If $H|A$ is sequentially consistent for each object $A$, then $H$ is linearizable.
C) If $H|A$ is linearizable for each object $A$, then $H$ is guaranteed only to be sequentially consistent, not necessarily linearizable.
D) If $H|A$ is linearizable for each object $A$, then $H$ is linearizable.
atom_statement: Linearizability is composable: if $H|A$ is linearizable for each object $A$, then $H$ is linearizable.
evidence: Linearizability has the useful property of being composable, in the sense that if H|A is linearizable for any particular object A, then H is linearizable.

question:
An atomic register initially holds 0. In an incomplete concurrent execution $H$, process $p$ has invoked write(1) and has not yet received a response. Process $r$ has invoked write(2) and has not yet received a response. Process $q$ invoked read and received the response 1. To linearize $H$, we extend $H$ by adding a response for $p$'s write(1) after $q$'s read response, giving $H'$. We then delete $r$'s unmatched invoke of write(2), giving $H''$. Finally we take the sequential execution $S$: $p$'s write(1), then $q$'s read returning 1.
Is $S$ a valid linearization of $H$ obtained through these steps? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: A linearization of a possibly incomplete concurrent execution $H$ is built in three steps: - Extend $H$ with zero or more response events to get $H'$. - Remove the invoke events in $H'$ that have no matching response to get $H''$. - Construct a sequential execution $S$ that meets the object's sequential specification, with $H''|p = S|p$ for all processes $p$ and $<_{H''} \subseteq <_S$.
evidence: implementation the ﬂexibility of deciding whether these operations have taken eﬀect or not, so given an incomplete concurrent execution H, a linearization of H involves three steps:
Extend H by adding zero or more response events, obtaining a new execution H′.
Remove any invoke events in H′ that don’t have a matching response event, obtaining a new execution H′′.
Construct a sequential S such that S meets the sequential speciﬁcation of the object, H′′|p = S|p for all p, and <H′′⊆<S.2

key_points: Sequential consistency is weaker: it requires only a sequential execution indistinguishable to all processes, dropping the requirement $<_H \subseteq <_S$
The sequential execution may order operations differently from the global (real-time) order, e.g. a read after a write may still return the earlier value
question: How does sequential consistency differ from linearizability in what it requires of the sequential execution, and what consequence does this have for the ordering of operations?
atom_statement: Sequential consistency is weaker than linearizability: it requires only a sequential execution indistinguishable to all processes, essentially dropping the requirement $<_H \subseteq <_S$. That sequential execution may therefore order operations differently from the global order.
evidence: This says that for any concurrent execution of the object, there exists some sequential execution that is indistinguishable to all processes; however, this sequential execution might include operations that occur out of order from a global perspective.

(Essentially we are dropping the requirement <H⊆<S from the linearizability deﬁnition.) For example, we could have an execution of an atomic register where you write to it, then I read from it, but I get the initial value that precedes your write.

question:
True or False?
"Linearizability of an implementation can usually be proved using only incomplete executions when the implementation guarantees that any operation in progress can eventually finish."
atom_statement: Linearizability of an implementation can usually be proved using only complete executions when the implementation guarantees that any operation in progress can eventually finish. In that case any incomplete $H$ can be extended to a complete $H' = H''$ by running pending operations to completion.
evidence: Even better, if we are asking if an implementation of an object is linearizable—meaning that all executions of the object are linearizable—then we can usually prove this by proving it only for complete executions, since if the implementation has the property that any operation in progress can eventually ﬁnish, we can extend any incomplete H to a complete H′ = H′′ by simply running any pending operations to completion.

question:
Two atomic registers $x$ and $y$ both start at 0. Process $p$ writes 1 to $x$ and then reads 0 from $y$. Process $q$ writes 1 to $y$ and then reads 0 from $x$. Together these operations form an execution $H$. The restriction $H|x$ is sequentially consistent and the restriction $H|y$ is sequentially consistent, but $H$ as a whole is not sequentially consistent.
Does sequential consistency satisfy the composability property (each per-object restriction being acceptable implies the whole execution is acceptable) on this execution? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: Sequential consistency does not generally have the composability property that linearizability has.
evidence: Sequential consistency does not generally have this property.

question: What round complexity does the Byzantine agreement algorithm based on exponential information gathering (EIG) achieve, and what condition relating the number of processes $n$ to the number of Byzantine faults $f$ must hold for it to guarantee agreement and validity?
atom_statement: EIG gives a Byzantine agreement algorithm that runs in $f+1$ synchronous rounds and guarantees agreement and validity as long as $n \ge 3f+1$.
evidence: 10.2.1 Exponential information gathering gets n = 3f + 1

This technique was used by Pease, Shostak, and Lamport [PSL80] to show that their impossibility result is tight: there exists an algorithm for Byzantine agreement that runs in f + 1 synchronous rounds and guarantees agreement and validity as long as n ≥3f + 1.

True or False?
"In exponential information gathering, each process's state is a tree built from pairs ⟨path, input⟩, where path is a sequence of intermediaries that may contain repeated processes."

evidence: The idea of exponential information gathering is that each process will do a lot of gossiping, but now its state is no longer just a ﬂat set of inputs, but a tree describing who it heard what from.
We build this tree out of pairs of the form ⟨path, input⟩where path is a sequence of intermediaries with no repetitions and input is some input.

A synchronous message-passing system has $n=7$ processes, of which at most $f=2$ may be Byzantine. The processes run a Byzantine agreement algorithm based on exponential information gathering, executing for $3$ rounds, and then each process decides.
Does this setup guarantee that the algorithm satisfies both agreement and validity? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: Exponential information gathering gives a synchronous Byzantine agreement algorithm that runs in $f+1$ rounds and guarantees agreement and validity as long as $n \ge 3f+1$.
evidence: This technique was used by Pease, Shostak, and Lamport [PSL80] to show that their impossibility result is tight: there exists an algorithm for Byzantine agreement that runs in f + 1 synchronous rounds and guarantees agreement and validity as long as n ≥3f + 1.

key_points: A common node is one where all non-faulty processes compute the same $val^*$

Every root-to-leaf path passes through $f+1$ labels, at least one good, so it contains a common node; a node whose children are all common is itself common, so a non-common root would give a path with no common node, which is impossible
question: In the correctness proof of the exponential information gathering Byzantine agreement algorithm, how is agreement established? Describe the notion of a common node and why the root must be common.
atom_statement: EIG achieves agreement through the notion of a common node, one where all non-faulty processes compute the same $val^*$. Every root-to-leaf path has a common node because it passes through $f+1$ labels and at least one is good. A node whose children are all common is itself common, so a non-common root would force a path with no common node, which is impossible.
evidence: Agreement: Observe that every path has a common node on it, since a path travels through f +1 nodes and one of them is good.
If we then suppose that the root is not common: by Lemma 10.2.3, it must have a not-common child, that node must have a not-common child, etc.
But this constructs a path from the root to a leaf with no not-common nodes, which we just proved can’t happen.

key_points: Not solvable: no algorithm exists for $n=3f$ (the $n=3$, $f=1$ case is impossible)
Reduction: each of 3 processes simulates a group of $f$ processes sharing the same input, so an $n=3f$ algorithm would give one for $n=3$, $f=1$
question: Is Byzantine agreement solvable with $n=3f$ processes, and what reduction argument shows this?
atom_statement: No algorithm can solve Byzantine agreement with $n=3f$ processes. The $n=3$, $f=1$ case is impossible, and a protocol for $n=3f$ would yield one for $n=3$, $f=1$ by letting each of 3 processes simulate a group of $f$ processes that all share the same input.
evidence: Suppose that there were an algorithm that solved Byzantine agreement with n = 3f processes.
Group the processes into groups of size f, and let each of the n = 3 processes simulate one group, with everybody in the group getting the same input, which can only make things easier.
Then we get a protocol for n = 3 and f = 1, an impossibility.

question: In the Jayanti-Tan-Toueg lower-bound argument, an object is called perturbable. Given an execution $\Lambda_k\Sigma_k$ and a reader's operation $\pi$, what must hold for the object to be perturbable?
atom_statement: An object is perturbable if, for an execution $\Lambda_k\Sigma_k$, a partial execution $\gamma$ always exists that can be inserted between $\Lambda_k$ and $\Sigma_k$ and changes what the reader's operation $\pi$ returns, so that $\Lambda_k\gamma\Sigma_k\pi$ returns something different from $\Lambda_k\gamma\Sigma_k$.
evidence: For the induction step, we start with ΛkΣk, and look for a partial execution γ that we can insert in between Λk and Σk that changes what π returns in ΛkγΣkπ from what it returned in ΛkγΣk.
This is where perturbability comes in: an object is deﬁned to be per- turbable if such a partial execution γ always exists.

"Historyless objects are those for which every operation either never changes the state or always sets the state to a value that depends on both the operation and the previous state."

evidence: Historyless objects are those for which any operation either never changes the state (like a read, but it could be weaker) or always sets the state to a value that depends only on the operation and not the previous

question:
A team claims to have a deterministic, solo-terminating implementation of a max register for $n = 8$ processes, built only from historyless objects (atomic registers). The implementation uses 5 registers in total, and a read operation takes at most 5 steps in every execution.
Is this implementation consistent with the Jayanti-Tan-Toueg lower bound for perturbable objects? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: The Jayanti-Tan-Toueg lower bound says that any solo-terminating deterministic implementation of a perturbable object (such as a counter, generalized counter, or max register) from historyless objects requires $n-1$ space and $n-1$ steps for a read operation in the worst case.
evidence: Unfortunately, the Jayanti-Tan-Toueg [JTT00] lower bound for per- turbable objects says each of these objects requires n −1 space and n −1 steps for a read operation in the worst case, for any solo-terminating deter- ministic implementation from historyless objects.

atom_statement: Repeating the induction step until $n-1$ objects are covered shows that at least $n-1$ objects are needed (the space bound) and that in the worst case some reader reads all of them (the step complexity bound).

question:
An implementation of a perturbable counter for $n = 6$ processes is deterministic and solo-terminating, and is built from historyless objects. It uses 5 registers, which meets the space bound. However, in every execution a read operation reads at most 2 of these registers.
Is this implementation consistent with the step-complexity bound obtained by repeating the Jayanti-Tan-Toueg induction step until $n-1$ objects are covered? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: S2 rank 3: Repeating the induction step until $n-1$ objects are covered implies at least $n-1$ objects exist, which is the space bound. In the worst case some reader reads all of them, which is the step-complexity bound.
evidence: We can repeat this step until we’ve covered n −1 objects.
This implies that there are at least n −1 objects (the space lower bound), and in the worst case some reader reads all of them (the step complexity lower bound).

A designer implements a counter from atomic registers for $n$ processes. The implementation is only required to work in executions where the total number of operations is bounded by a fixed length $m$ known in advance.

question:
A shared-memory system has $n=5$ processes. Each process runs the same kind of loop: it takes a snapshot of a shared array, then writes an update to its own array entry, then takes another snapshot, then writes another update, and so on. Each process always alternates strictly between snapshots and updates. Each update value is computed from the preceding snapshot. A team wants to run this system as the simulated system in a BG simulation.
Does the structure of these simulated processes match what the BG simulation assumes about simulated processes, so that each process's behavior is determined by the sequence of snapshots it receives? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: The BG simulation assumes that all simulated processes alternate between taking snapshots and doing updates, so the actions of a simulated process can be determined by determining the sequence of snapshots it receives.
evidence: To avoid having to simulate speciﬁc choices of operations, the BG simulation assumes that all simulated processes alternate between taking snapshots and doing updates.
This approach means that we can determine the actions of some simulated process by determining the sequence of snapshots that it receives.

question:
A BG simulation uses 4 simulating processes ($t=3$) to simulate 10 processes. For each simulated process $j$ and each step $r$, the simulators use a safe agreement object $S_{jr}$. atom_statement: Because each simulating process is in the unsafe interval of at most one safe agreement object at a time, the crash of a simulating process can stall at most one safe agreement object and hence knocks out at most one simulated process.

question:
A system of 3 simulating processes simulates 5 processes, with up to 2 crashes. In the simulation, each simulator simply returns the output of whichever simulated process happens to decide first. No simulator is tied to any particular simulated process. A crash of a simulator may stall any simulated process, and nothing guarantees that a particular simulated process survives as long as its simulator does. The team intends to use this to solve renaming, where simulators must output distinct names.
Does this simulation overcome the colorless-task restriction in the way the extended BG simulation does? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: The extended BG simulation addresses the colorless-task restriction by mapping each simulating process $p$ to a specific simulated process $q_p$ and guaranteeing that $q_p$ does not crash unless $p$ does.

question:
Consider the Dirichlet form of a graph Laplacian on the infinite graph $\mathbb Z$ with generic edge weights $b$ and vertex measure $m$. This is a non-local Dirichlet form. atom_statement: For a non-local Dirichlet form, including the setting of graph Laplacians, there is in general no largest intrinsic metric, so no canonical choice of intrinsic metric can be made, unlike for strongly local forms where the classical intrinsic metric is the largest intrinsic metric.
evidence: One of the crucial differences is that it is no longer possible to associate a unique intrinsic metric to a general Dirichlet form.

For a non-local Dirichlet form (including the setting of graph Laplacians), there is in general no largest intrinsic metric and hence it is not possible to make a canonical choice.

question:
Let $X$ be a simplicial set in which every inner horn $\Lambda^k[n]\to X$ ($0<k<n$) has a filler $\Delta[n]\to X$. One wants to describe its homotopy category $\tau(X)$, which is defined abstractly by generators and relations.
Is $X$ a case where $\tau(X)$ admits a much easier explicit description than for a general simplicial set? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: For a general simplicial set $X$ the category $\tau(X)$ is hard to control because it is defined only by generators and relations. It becomes much easier to describe when $X$ is an inner Kan complex.

evidence: Corollary 5.51 Let Y be an ∞-category.
Then the following are equivalent:
(i) Y is a Kan complex, (ii) τ(Y) is a groupoid, (iii) Y →∆[0] is a left ﬁbration, (iv) Y →∆[0] is a right ﬁbration.

question:
True or False?
"For an inner fibration $f:Y\to X$ between ∞-categories, the fact that $k(f):k(Y)\to k(X)$ is a Kan fibration does not imply that $\tau(f)$ is an isofibration; there can be such $f$ where $\tau(f)$ fails to be an isofibration."
atom_statement: For an inner fibration $f:Y\to X$ between ∞-categories, the following are equivalent: $k(f):k(Y)\to k(X)$ is a Kan fibration, $\tau(f)$ is an isofibration, $f$ has J-path lifting, and $f$ has path lifting with respect to equivalences.
evidence: Corollary 5.54 Let f : Y →X be an inner ﬁbration between ∞-categories.
Then the following properties are equivalent:
(i) k( f ): k(Y) →k(X) is a Kan ﬁbration, (ii) τ( f ): τ(Y) →τ(X) is an isoﬁbration, (iii) f has J-path lifting, (iv) f has path lifting with respect to equivalences.

question:
Let $Y=\Delta[1]$ (the nerve of the poset $0<1$, an ∞-category) and $X=\Delta[0]$ (a Kan complex), and let $f:Y\to X$ be the unique map. It is an inner fibration, since $Y$ is an ∞-category. The non-identity arrow $0\to1$ in $Y$ is sent by $f$ to the identity of the unique vertex of $X$.
Is $f$ a Kan fibration? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: For an inner fibration $f:Y\to X$ with $X$ a Kan complex, $f$ is a Kan fibration if and only if $\tau(f)$ is a conservative isofibration, if and only if $f$ is a left fibration, if and only if $f$ is a right fibration.

(i) f is a Kan ﬁbration, (ii) τ( f ) is a conservative isoﬁbration, (iii) f is a left ﬁbration,

question:
True or False?
"In the category $\Omega$ the objects are trees, and a morphism $S \to T$ is a map of operads in Sets from the operad $\Omega(S)$ generated by $S$ to the operad $\Omega(T)$ generated by $T$; consequently $\Omega$ is a full subcategory of the category of operads in Sets."
atom_statement: The category Ω has trees as objects and, as morphisms S → T, maps of operads Ω(S) → Ω(T) between the operads in Sets generated by the trees, so Ω is a full subcategory of the category of operads in Sets.
evidence: Deﬁnition 3.3 The category Ωis the category whose objects are trees and whose morphisms S →T are maps of operads Ω(S) →Ω(T).
Thus, by deﬁnition, Ωis a full subcategory of the category of operads in Sets.

question:
Let $T$ be the corolla with leaves $a, b$, a single vertex, and root edge $c$. Someone proposes an operad $P$ whose colours are exactly the edges $a, b, c$ of $T$. $P$ has only identity operations apart from the sets $P(a,b;c)$, which contains two distinct operations, and $P(b,a;c)$, which is empty.
Is $P$ the operad $\Omega(T)$ associated to the tree $T$? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: The operad Ω(T) associated to a tree T has the edges of T as its colours, and each set of operations Ω(T)(e_1,...,e_n;e) is either empty or a singleton, being nonempty exactly when T has a subtree with leaves e_1,...,e_n and root e.
evidence: The colours of Ω(T) are the edges of T.
Given a sequence of colours e1, . . ., en, e, the set of operations Ω(T)(e1, . . ., en; e) is either empty or a singleton.
There is an operation in Ω(T)(e1, . . ., en; e) if and only if there exists a subtree of T with leaves e1, . . ., en and root e.

question:
Let $T$ be a tree and $e$ an edge of $T$. Let $\sigma_e T$ be the tree obtained by splitting $e$ into two edges $e_1$ (above) and $e_2$ (below) with a new unary vertex $v$ between them. What does the elementary degeneracy $\sigma_e:\sigma_e T\to T$ do?
A) It sends both $e_1$ and $e_2$ to $e$, and sends the new unary vertex $v$ to the identity operation of colour $e$ in $\Omega(T)$.
B) It sends $e_2$ to $e$ and sends $e_1$ to the edge of $T$ directly above $e$, and sends $v$ to the identity operation of colour $e$ in $\Omega(T)$.
C) It sends $e_1$ to $e$ and sends $e_2$ to the root edge of $T$, and sends $v$ to the identity operation of colour $e$ in $\Omega(T)$.
D) It sends both $e_1$ and $e_2$ to $e$, and sends $v$ to the operation of the vertex of $T$ whose output edge is $e$.

question:
Let $S$ be the binary corolla with leaves $a, b$ and root $c$. Let $T$ be the tree with a vertex $w$ having leaves $a,b$ and output edge $d$, and a unary vertex $v$ with input $d$ and root edge $c$. question:
True or False?
"If $T$ is a closed tree, then every map of posets $\varphi: E(S)\to E(T)$ that preserves the incomparability relation $\perp$ on edges is the underlying edge map of a unique morphism $S\to T$ in $\Omega$."
atom_statement: If T is a closed tree, then any map of posets φ : E(S) → E(T) that preserves the incomparability relation ⊥ is the underlying edge map of a unique morphism S → T in Ω; correspondingly, the category of closed trees is equivalent to the category of finite posets with a unique maximal element satisfying the linear-order condition (∗) on the sets E_{e≤}, with maps of posets respecting incomparability.
evidence: Proposition 3.5 Let S and T be trees and let ϕ : E(S) →E(T) be a map of posets which preserves the incomparability relation ⊥on edges.
If T is closed, then ϕ is the underlying map on edges of a unique morphism S →T in Ω.

Indeed, since L(T) =  for a closed tree T, one concludes that Ωis equivalent to the category whose objects are ﬁnite posets satisfying the assumptions of 3.2 and whose morphisms are the maps of posets which respect the incomparability relation.

question:
Let $S$ be the binary corolla with leaves $a, b$ and root $c$. Let $T$ be the tree with two vertices: a vertex $v$ with inputs $a$ and $d$ and output $c$, and a unary vertex $w$ with input $b$ and output $d$. So $T$ contains a subtree with leaves $a, b$ and root $c$ that is obtained by grafting $w$ onto $v$ along $d$. Consider a map of operads $\Omega(S)\to\Omega(T)$ that is the identity on the colours $a,b,c$.
Does such a morphism $S\to T$ exist in $\Omega$, sending the operation in $\Omega(S)(a,b;c)$ to the composition $v\circ_d w$? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: Taking the interior of a tree is not a functor on Ω: there is no morphism from a binary corolla with leaves a, b and root c to a tree where an additional leaf d is present on the vertex, since there is no binary operation in the target to receive the binary operation, whereas a morphism exists into the tree with an extra vertex w, sending the operation to the composition v ∘_d w.
evidence: In fact, there is no such morphism in Ω.
Indeed, the binary operation in Ω(S)(a, b; c) would have to map to a binary operation in Ω(T), but there are none.
It sends the unique operation in Ω(S)(a, b; c) to the composition v◦d w.
This example shows that taking the interior of a tree is not a functor.

key_points: There is a homotopy $h:J\times B\to X$ from $f$ to $g$
The homotopy restricts to the constant homotopy on $A$
Composing $h$ with $p$ gives the constant homotopy $J\times B\to B\to S$
question: Let $p:X\to S$ be a J-fibration and $A\to B$ a monomorphism. What does it mean for two maps $f,g:B\to X$ with $pf=pg$ to be fibrewise J-homotopic relative to $A$?
atom_statement: For a J-fibration $p:X\to S$ and a monomorphism $A\to B$, two maps $f,g:B\to X$ with $pf=pg$ are fibrewise J-homotopic relative to $A$ if there is a homotopy $h:J\times B\to X$ from $f$ to $g$ that restricts to the constant homotopy on $A$ and whose composite with $p$ is the constant homotopy $J\times B\to B\to S$.
evidence: For a J-ﬁbration p : X →S and a monomorphism i : A →B, we call two maps f, g : B →X over S (i.e., p f = pg) ﬁbrewise J-homotopic relative to A if there is a homotopy h : J × B →X from f to g which restricts to the constant homotopy J × A →A →X on A and composes to the constant homotopy J × B →B →S to S.

question:
True or False?
"A J-fibration $p:X\to S$ between ∞-operads is a minimal J-fibration if, for any two dendrices $x,y\in X_T$ that are fibrewise J-homotopic relative to $\partial\Omega[T]$, the identity $\alpha^*x=y$ holds for every automorphism $\alpha$ of the tree $T$."
atom_statement: For a J-fibration $p:X\to S$ between ∞-operads, $p$ is a minimal J-fibration if for any two dendrices $x,y\in X_T$ that are fibrewise J-homotopic relative to $\partial\Omega[T]$ (fibrewise J-equivalent), there exists an automorphism $\alpha$ of the tree $T$ with $\alpha^*x=y$.
evidence: (a) Two dendrices x, y ∈XT are ﬁbrewise J-equivalent if, when viewed as maps Ω[T] →X, they are ﬁbrewise J-homotopic relative to the boundary ∂Ω[T].

(In particular, px = py and x and y agree on ∂Ω[T].) (b) The map p : X →S is a minimal J-ﬁbration if for any two ﬁbrewise J-equivalent dendrices x, y ∈XT, there exists an automorphism α of T so that α∗x = y.

question:
Let $S$ be the singular simplicial set of the circle, which is a Kan complex. Let $p=\mathrm{id}_S:S\to S$ be the identity map, which is a Kan fibration between simplicial sets.
Is $p$ a minimal Kan fibration? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: For a J-fibration $p:X\to S$ between ∞-categories (or a Kan fibration between general simplicial sets), $p$ is a minimal J-fibration (respectively a minimal Kan fibration) if any two fibrewise J-equivalent $n$-simplices of $X$, meaning fibrewise J-homotopic relative to $\partial\Delta[n]$ when viewed as maps $\Delta[n]\to X$, are equal.
evidence: Deﬁnition 5.69 Let p : X →S be a J-ﬁbration between ∞-categories or a Kan ﬁbration between general simplicial sets.
(a) Two n-simplices x, y ∈Xn are ﬁbrewise J-equivalent if, when viewed as maps ∆[n] →X, these simplices are ﬁbrewise J-homotopic relative to ∂∆[n].

(In particular, px = py and x and y agree on ∂∆[n].) (b) The map p : X →S is a minimal J-ﬁbration (or a minimal Kan ﬁbration if p is a Kan ﬁbration) if any two ﬁbrewise J-equivalent simplices are equal.

key_points: There exists a minimal J-fibration $q:M\to S$ that is a fibrewise J-deformation retract of $X\to S$
The retraction is a trivial fibration
question: Given a J-fibration $p:X\to S$ between ∞-categories, what can be said about the existence of a minimal J-fibration related to it, and what kind of map is the associated retraction?
atom_statement: For a J-fibration $p:X\to S$ between ∞-categories there exists a minimal J-fibration $q:M\to S$ that is a fibrewise J-deformation retract of $X\to S$, and the retraction is a trivial fibration; the same holds for a Kan fibration between arbitrary simplicial sets.
evidence: Theorem 5.71 Let p : X →S be a J-ﬁbration between ∞-categories.
Then there exists a minimal J-ﬁbration q : M →S which is a ﬁbrewise J-deformation retract of X →S.
Moreover, the retraction is a trivial ﬁbration.
The same applies to a Kan ﬁbration between arbitrary simplicial sets.

question:
Let $X\to S$ and $Y\to S$ be minimal J-fibrations between ∞-categories, and let $\varphi:X\to Y$ be a map over $S$. Which statement is correct?
A) If $\varphi$ is a fibrewise J-homotopy equivalence over $S$, then $\varphi$ is an isomorphism.
B) Every map $\varphi:X\to Y$ over $S$ is an isomorphism, whether or not it is a fibrewise J-homotopy equivalence.
C) The conclusion that a fibrewise J-homotopy equivalence $\varphi$ is an isomorphism holds for arbitrary J-fibrations $X\to S$ and $Y\to S$, not only minimal ones.
D) If $\varphi$ is a fibrewise J-homotopy equivalence over $S$, then $\varphi$ is a trivial fibration but need not be an isomorphism.
atom_statement: Any fibrewise J-homotopy equivalence $\varphi:X\to Y$ over $S$ between two minimal J-fibrations $X\to S$ and $Y\to S$ of $\infty$-categories is an isomorphism, and the same holds for minimal Kan fibrations between general simplicial sets.
evidence: Proposition 5.70 Let p : X →S and q : Y →S be minimal J-ﬁbrations between ∞-categories.
Then any ﬁbrewise J-homotopy equivalence ϕ : X →Y over S is an isomorphism.
The same is true for minimal Kan ﬁbrations between general simplicial sets.

key_points: The induced maps of stabilizers $\mathrm{Aut}(T)_x\to\mathrm{Aut}(T)_{f(x)}$ must be isomorphisms for all dendrices $x$
This is automatic when $S'$ and $S$ are normal
question: For dendroidal sets, let $p:X\to S$ be a minimal J-fibration of ∞-operads with $X$ normal, and let $f:S'\to S$ be a map of ∞-operads. Under what condition on $f$ is the pullback $f^*X\to S'$ guaranteed to be a minimal J-fibration, and when is this condition automatic?
atom_statement: For simplicial sets, minimal J-fibrations are readily closed under pullback, but for dendroidal sets pullback along a map $f:S'\to S$ of $\infty$-operads preserves minimality of a minimal J-fibration $p:X\to S$ with $X$ normal only when the induced maps of stabilizers $\mathrm{Aut}(T)_x\to\mathrm{Aut}(T)_{f(x)}$ are isomorphisms, a condition automatically satisfied when $S'$ and $S$ are normal.
evidence: In the case of simplicial sets it was rather evident that the class of minimal J- ﬁbrations is closed under pullbacks.
This is not quite the case for dendroidal sets.
Lemma 6.57 Let f : S′ →S be a map of ∞-operads such that for any dendrex x ∈XT, the induced map of stabilizers Aut(T)x →Aut(T)f (x) is an isomorphism.
If p : X →S is a minimal J-ﬁbration between ∞-operads, with X normal, then the pullback q : f ∗X →S′ is again a minimal J-ﬁbration between ∞-operads.
In particular, note that the condition on stabilizers is automatically satisﬁed when S′ and S are normal.

question:
True or False?
"The result that any fibrewise J-homotopy equivalence over $S$ between minimal J-fibrations $X\to S$ and $Y\to S$ of ∞-operads is an isomorphism is proved under the hypothesis that both $X$ and $Y$ are normal."
atom_statement: The dendroidal rigidity result (any fibrewise J-homotopy equivalence over $S$ between minimal J-fibrations $X\to S$ and $Y\to S$ of ∞-operads is an isomorphism) requires both $X$ and $Y$ to be normal.
evidence: Proposition 6.54 Let p : X →S and q : Y →S be minimal J-ﬁbrations between ∞-operads and suppose both X and Y are normal.
Then any ﬁbrewise J-homotopy equivalence X →Y over S is an isomorphism.

question:
What is the target of direct T-cell alloreactivity?
A) Intact mismatched HLA–peptide complexes expressed on the cell surface of autologous (self) cells
B) Intact mismatched HLA–peptide complexes expressed on the cell surface of allogeneic cells
C) Peptides derived from mismatched HLA proteins and presented in the antigen-binding groove of self-HLA molecules
D) Intact HLA–peptide complexes that are fully matched between donor and recipient on the cell surface of allogeneic cells
atom_statement: Direct T-cell alloreactivity is targeted to intact mismatched HLA–peptide complexes expressed on the cell surface of allogeneic cells.
evidence: Direct T-cell alloreactivity is targeted next-generation sequencing to intact mismatched HLA–peptide complexes expressed on the cell surface of allogeneic cells and can be mediated by both naïve and memory T cells (Archbold et al. 2008).

question:
After an HLA-matched allogeneic HCT, donor T cells recognize a peptide that is derived from a polymorphic intracellular protein encoded by a non-HLA gene. Does this peptide qualify as a minor histocompatibility antigen (mHAg)? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: Minor histocompatibility antigens (mHAgs) are foreign peptides that derive not from mismatched HLA but from other expressed polymorphic genes, and that are presented by self-HLA molecules.
evidence: mismatched HLA but from any other expressed polymorphic gene and presented by self-HLA molecules.

key_points: Minor histocompatibility antigens (mHAgs)
They are the only targets in the HLA-matched setting
question: In HLA-matched allogeneic HCT, which antigens are the only targets of T-cell alloreactivity?
atom_statement: In HLA-matched allo-HCT, minor histocompatibility antigens (mHAgs) are the only targets of T-cell alloreactivity.
evidence: These peptides are referred to as minor histocompatibility antigens (mHAgs) (Spierings 2014); mHAgs are the only targets of T-cell alloreactivity in HLA-matched allo-HCT and are mainly recognized by naïve T cells.

question: How is the pathophysiology of acute graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) conceptualized as a three-phase process? Name the phases in order and describe what characterizes each.
atom_statement: The pathophysiology of acute GvHD has been attributed to a three-phase process. Tissue damage from the conditioning regimen comes first, then an afferent phase of host antigen-presenting cell activation and donor T-cell activation and proliferation, then an efferent phase of effector damage.
evidence: The pathophysiology of aGvHD has been attributed to a three-phase process comprising initial tissue damage from the conditioning regimen which in turn leads to activation of host antigen-presenting cells by pathogen- associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) and activation and proliferation of donor T cells (afferent phase) and finally to the effector phase characterized by cytotoxic cell damage and release of inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1 (IL-1) and tissue necrosis factor-alpha (TNFα) that eventually produce tissue necrosis (efferent phase).

evidence: However, still, some track structure codes use atomic ionization/electronic excitation cross sections [58] obtained in the gas phase even if, in principle, they are not suitable for low energy excitations of valence electrons in water, since such excitations are sensitive to the electronic structure of the target [54, 59–61].

question:
True or False?
"Low-energy interaction cross sections depend on the composition of a medium but not on its physical state, so gas-phase and condensed-phase cross sections are the same."
atom_statement: Low-energy interaction cross sections depend on the state of the medium as well as its composition, so gas-phase and condensed-phase cross sections differ, and experimental cross sections for biological media in the condensed state are very difficult to obtain, with only a few data under specific conditions existing for liquid water.
evidence: An important point to consider is that at these low energies, the interaction cross sections depend on the composition of the material but also on its state.
That is to say that the cross sections are not the same for a medium in a gaseous or a solid state.
This leads to a particular difficulty because it is very difficult (not to say, almost impossible) to obtain experimental cross sections for biological media in their condensed state [24].

Only a few data obtained under very specific conditions exist for liquid water [56, 57] and these data are the basis for the set of models utilized to calculate the cross sections used by most track structure codes.

question:
A dose calculation code for therapeutic-energy proton beams in a patient CT transports particles in steps of about 1 mm. Each step stands for many individual elastic and inelastic collisions, combined using multiple-scattering theory, and the energy loss is applied continuously along the step.
Is this code an instance of condensed-history Monte Carlo, which lacks the nanoscale resolution of event-by-event track structure simulation? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: Condensed-history Monte Carlo, which groups many scattering events into fewer artificial steps much longer than the particle mean free path with continuous energy loss, is used for dosimetry and most microdosimetry of very energetic particles but lacks the nanoscale resolution that event-by-event track structure simulation provides.
evidence: As we described earlier in this chapter, particle transport through matter using MC codes is generally handled via a “condensed history” (CH) approach [53], currently used for dosimetry and the majority of microdosimetry applications for very energetic particles.

In such a CH approach, many scattering events are grouped into fewer artificial steps, much longer than the mean free path of the particle, using multiple-scattering theories and a continuous energy loss along those steps.

However, in order to simulate the physics at the nanoscale and to possibly link it to the biological effects of radiation with track structure properties in the nm regime [54], an event-by-event tracking of the different physical events is necessary to allow for better spatial resolution.

question:
Asynchronously cycling mammalian cells receive a first radiation fraction. The surviving cells are kept in culture at 37 °C and receive a second identical fraction after an interval of 0, 2, 4 or 6 h. Clonogenic survival is measured for each interval.
Is survival expected to decrease as the interval between the fractions increases? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: In split-dose experiments at 37 °C, cells continue through the cell cycle after the first fraction and reach a maximally radiosensitive stage. Survival therefore decreases as the time between fractions increases. At 24 °C the cells stay in a resistant stage, so their radiosensitivity stays constant between fractions.
evidence: At 24 °C, surviving cells stay in the stage of the cell cycle where they are resistant between the dose fractions and therefore their radiosensitivity is constant with time.

At 37 °C, they continue through the cell cycle after the first frac tion and at some time later will have reached a cell cycle stage where they have maximum radiosensitivity, whereupon the second dose fraction is given.
Consequently, survival as a function of the time between fractions will decrease with increasing time.

question: What type of chromosomal translocations do cells exposed to high-LET particle radiation mostly suffer, and what produces them?
